answers.question: Does turning off the fans put out a fire in Moon Base air?
answers.answer: Not reliably, and no study here tests it directly in Moon Base air. BASS-II found flames always quenched when the fan was turned off (ICES-2019-101, page 1), but only up to 22.2% oxygen, below Moon Base levels (BASS-II card caveats). ACME BRE flames burned with no airflow at all: in 21% oxygen they self-extinguished within 40 s, but at 27% oxygen/10.2 psia and 34% oxygen/8.2 psia they generally persisted 3 minutes or more (BRE Final Report, pages 40 and 18). Saffire IV/V found extinguishment in still air 'cannot be assumed to occur rapidly' (ICES-2021-266, page 11). Our note: this suggests fans off alone is not a safe assumption.

answers.question: What tests exist at 30% oxygen or more and low pressure?
answers.answer: Few tests, mostly gas or droplet flames, not cabin materials. ACME CFI-G (PSI table, tests_by_zone): 20 tests inside the zone, 33.2-39.3% oxygen at 0.51 bar (about 7.3 psi); 17 flames ignited, median 62 s. ACME BRE: test 19070D1, 34% oxygen at 8.2 psia, steady burning with no airflow (BRE Final Report, page 18). Saffire-VI: VI-2 and VI-3, about 29-31% oxygen at about 54-55 kPa (Urban et al., ICES-2024-365). FLEX: 17 edge tests, 30-34% oxygen at 10.3-10.5 psi, just above the 10.2 psi limit. BASS-II tested only up to 22.2% oxygen.

answers.question: Which materials behaved differently in microgravity than on Earth?
answers.answer: Silicone: in Saffire-II's microgravity burns it did not spread in any of four samples, though two burned completely in the 1-g comparison (Saffire-II, PSI-99 table, lines 2-5). PMMA: BASS-II found it burns at lower oxygen in microgravity, a flammability boundary bottoming at about 13.5% oxygen versus 15.4% for upward burning on Earth (BASS-II, Summary Report, page 84). Smoke: SAME found low-gravity smoke particles typically 50% larger than on Earth (SAME final report, page 66). Gas flames: ACME CLD found 5-8 times more soot in microgravity (ACME overview, page 4). Caveat: these come from different tests and conditions.

answers.question: Can a flame relight after it seems to go out?
answers.answer: Yes, in some droplet experiments. The Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) reports that above about 2 atm, flames often relit on their own, "multiple reignition cycles" where a hot flame goes out from radiative heat loss, a cool flame follows, and then a hot flame reignites, repeating until the fuel droplet is gone (CFI, Science Final Report, page 6). Warm flames also appeared after radiative extinction, and the flame is not visible in the color camera (page 8). Caveats: the CFI data isn't fully analyzed, and Moon Base pressure (about 0.7 atm) is far lower, so this is not Moon Base evidence. ACME Flame Design (final report, page 26) also notes a flame may partially extinguish and then reform before complete extinction.

answers.question: How long does smoke take to reach a detector on the ISS?
answers.answer: The digest gives no single detection time. SAME's computer model of the ISS US Lab found that "detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity" and "actual detection times can be quite long and strongly dependent on location and the presence of obstructions" (Urban et al., SAME final science report, page 4 and page 66). In some low-smoke cases a detector never alarmed in the 300 s simulated, after a 30 s source delay (SAME card; page 65). SAME-R's report (SAMER Final Report, page 5) does not give transport times. The SAME model used normal station ventilation.
